title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 28
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A quarry installed dust suppression equipment and reports that complaints from nearby residents have fallen by 80 per cent. Management concludes that dust levels have fallen correspondingly.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The equipment operates only during blasting.
B. The quarry simultaneously introduced a compensation scheme requiring residents to submit complaints through a form obtainable from its office.
C. Dust is measured by monitors at the site boundary.
D. The equipment was expensive to install.
E. Residents were consulted about the design.
questions.explanation: Raising the effort required to complain reduces complaints without reducing dust, so the proxy has been changed rather than the thing it stood for.

questions.prompt: A dance school reports that pupils who take part in its annual show progress to higher grades faster than those who do not, and plans to require all pupils to take part.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. The show is staged in a hired theatre.
B. The show runs for two nights.
C. Some pupils are nervous of performing.
D. Pupils volunteer for the show when they are already committed enough to attend extra rehearsals, and those rehearsals are additional teaching time.
E. Grades are assessed by an external examiner.
questions.explanation: Both commitment and the extra teaching are confounded with participation, and compulsion transfers neither.

questions.prompt: A greengrocer began displaying produce in wooden crates rather than on plastic shelving and reports that sales of fruit rose 12 per cent. The owner concludes that customers prefer produce displayed in crates.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How much the crates cost
B. Whether the crates are made from sustainable timber
C. Whether the crates hold more produce, so that fruit is now displayed in larger quantity and replenished more often
D. How long the shop has traded
E. Whether vegetables are displayed the same way
questions.explanation: Volume and freshness of display drive produce sales independently of the container's appearance, and the two changed together.

questions.prompt: An air ambulance charity reports that patients it airlifts have better survival rates than patients with similar injuries taken by road, and argues that its service saves lives.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the argument?
options: A. Helicopters cannot fly in fog.
B. The charity is funded by donations.
C. Crews include a doctor as well as paramedics.
D. Road ambulances are more numerous.
E. Dispatchers send the helicopter to patients judged to have the best prospect of surviving a long transfer, and send road ambulances to those too unstable to move.
questions.explanation: Triage assigns the two groups on precisely the characteristic the comparison is meant to measure, so the survival gap may exist before any transport occurs.

questions.prompt: Every garment altered by the Ashwood tailor that uses hand-finished buttonholes is made from cloth woven in Britain. No garment made from British-woven cloth has been returned for repair this year. Some garments altered by the tailor have been returned for repair this year.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Some garments altered by the tailor do not use hand-finished buttonholes.
B. Hand-finished buttonholes are more durable.
C. Most garments use British-woven cloth.
D. British cloth is more expensive.
E. Returned garments were altered recently.
questions.explanation: Returned garments are not made from British cloth, and hand-finished buttonholes imply that cloth, so those garments have machine-finished buttonholes.

questions.prompt: A locksmith advertises that fitting its high-security locks reduces the chance of a break-in, citing that fewer than 1 per cent of homes it has fitted have been burgled, compared with a national rate of 3 per cent.
questions.question: The advertisement is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. does not specify the period over which burglaries were counted
B. compares customers who chose to invest in security with the general population
C. ignores the cost of the locks
D. relies on figures the locksmith collected itself
E. overlooks burglaries that were attempted but failed
questions.explanation: Households that buy high-security locks differ in area, alarm use and behaviour; the comparison is not between like and like.

questions.prompt: A bookshop introduced a table of staff recommendations and reports that titles on the table outsell those on the ordinary shelves by a wide margin. It concludes that staff recommendations drive sales.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The table is placed near the entrance and holds twelve titles, all displayed face out.
B. The table is refreshed monthly.
C. Some customers ask staff for advice.
D. Staff choose books they have read.
E. The shop also sells stationery.
questions.explanation: Position and face-out display raise sales for almost any title, so the endorsement is confounded with the prominence.

questions.prompt: A swimming club reports that members who train in the early morning squad record faster times than those in the evening squad, and proposes moving all competitive swimmers to the morning.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the proposal?
options: A. The morning squad is selected by the coach from swimmers who have already met qualifying times.
B. The pool is warmer in the evening.
C. Evening sessions are more crowded.
D. Some swimmers attend both squads.
E. Times are recorded electronically.
questions.explanation: The morning squad's speed is its entry condition, so moving everyone there cannot reproduce the difference.

questions.prompt: A window cleaning firm switched from ladders to a water-fed pole system and reports that its insurance premiums fell by a third. The owner concludes that the new system is safer.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The poles are lighter than ladders.
B. The system was expensive to buy.
C. The insurer's premium is calculated from the firm's own claims history, and reported falls from height fell to zero in the two years after the change.
D. Customers prefer the new method.
E. Staff required training to use the poles.
questions.explanation: It links the premium to the firm's own accident record rather than to an insurer's general classification, which is what the safety claim needs.

questions.prompt: A seed merchant reports that customers who buy its premium compost achieve better germination rates than those who buy the standard grade, and advertises the premium compost as improving germination.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advertisement?
options: A. The premium compost costs twice as much.
B. Both grades are sold in the same size bags.
C. The merchant also sells seed trays.
D. Germination is tested in spring.
E. Germination rates are reported by customers, and those who spend more on compost are more likely to be experienced growers who also sow at the right depth and temperature.
questions.explanation: The purchase marks the grower's expertise, and the outcome is self-reported by that same group, so two biases run in the same direction.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to close a rural primary school argue that its cost per pupil is three times the national average. Opponents reply that closure would require the youngest children to travel forty minutes each way by bus.
questions.question: The opponents' reply functions in the argument by
options: A. disputing the cost figure the supporters cite
B. identifying a cost of the proposal that the per-pupil comparison does not capture
C. arguing that small schools produce better results
D. questioning the motives of the supporters
E. proposing an alternative source of funding
questions.explanation: The reply grants the arithmetic and points to a burden borne by children and families rather than by the education budget.

questions.passageText:
Firms that cannot measure an individual's output precisely often pay by rank instead: the employee judged best is promoted, and the reward is the difference between the two salaries. This is a tournament, and it has properties that ordinary pay-for-output does not.

Its advantage is robustness to noise that affects everyone. If a whole department has a bad year for reasons outside anyone's control, a bonus tied to results falls for all of them; a promotion still goes to whoever performed best. Relative judgement filters out the common shock, and it requires only that the employer rank employees, not that it measure them.

The costs follow from the same feature. Because the prize goes to whoever finishes ahead, an employee can win by performing better or by ensuring that colleagues perform worse, and the second is often cheaper. Cooperation, mentoring and the sharing of information are precisely what a tournament discourages, which is why firms most dependent on collaboration tend to flatten the prize or judge teams rather than individuals.

There is a subtler effect on who competes. A tournament rewards variance: an employee behind on current form does better to take a risk than to perform steadily, since finishing second is worth nothing. The same structure that motivates effort therefore encourages gambling by those unlikely to win, and discourages effort altogether once a contest looks decided — which is why long promotion cycles with a single obvious front-runner produce the least effort from everyone else, exactly when the firm most needs it.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a tournament is robust to noise because
options: A. employees are paid the same regardless of results
B. output is measured precisely
C. relative judgement filters out shocks affecting everyone
D. promotions occur at fixed intervals
E. the prize is small relative to salary
questions.explanation: A bad year for the whole department lowers everyone's results, but the promotion still goes to whoever performed best.

questions.passageText:
General anaesthesia is administered millions of times a year with a safety record that is among modern medicine's genuine achievements. What it does to produce unconsciousness is not fully understood, and the gap between reliable use and secure explanation is instructive.

The oldest account observed that the potency of an anaesthetic tracks its solubility in oil almost across the whole range of agents, suggesting the drugs act by dissolving into cell membranes and disturbing them. The correlation is striking and has survived; the mechanism inferred from it has not, because compounds have been found that fit the solubility relation and produce no anaesthesia, which a purely physical membrane effect does not predict.

Current accounts focus instead on specific proteins — receptors and ion channels that certain agents demonstrably bind. This is better supported and less tidy: different anaesthetics act on different targets, so there is no single mechanism, and drugs that produce apparently identical clinical states may do so by different routes.

The harder problem is the endpoint. Unconsciousness is not the absence of brain activity but a change in how activity is organised, and identifying which change constitutes it requires deciding what consciousness consists of — a question anaesthesia research inherits rather than solves. This is why depth of anaesthesia is monitored by proxies whose relation to awareness is statistical rather than definitional, and why the rare cases of awareness under anaesthesia remain difficult both to predict and to detect.
questions.prompt: The oldest account of anaesthetic action rested on the observation that potency tracks
options: A. molecular weight
B. the rate of metabolism in the liver
C. binding to a single receptor type
D. the volume administered
E. solubility in oil
questions.explanation: The correlation has survived; what has not is the membrane mechanism inferred from it.

questions.passageText:
Children in a school year differ in age by up to twelve months, and in the early years that difference is a substantial fraction of a life. The younger ones perform worse on average, which is unsurprising, and the pattern's persistence is not.

The effect is measurable in attainment throughout primary school, in the probability of being identified as having a special educational need, and — most strikingly — in selection for competitive sport, where the distribution of professional players' birth months is skewed toward the start of the selection year in country after country. A twelve-year-old who is nearly a year older is bigger and better coordinated, is selected for the better team, receives better coaching, and the initial advantage compounds into one that is no longer about age at all.

The academic effect fades with time but does not vanish before it has done work: judgements made about a six-year-old shape what that child is offered, and streaming by apparent ability early in school converts a maturity difference into a durable one.

The remedies are unsatisfying. Age-adjusting test scores addresses measurement but not the coaching and streaming that follow from it. Later selection helps in sport and is resisted by those who benefit from the current arrangement. And any cut-off produces a boundary, so the problem cannot be abolished, only made less consequential — which is an argument for reducing how much rests on early judgements rather than for finding a better date.
questions.prompt: The passage cites the distribution of professional players' birth months as evidence that
options: A. age differences within a school year vanish quickly
B. coaching quality is unrelated to selection
C. sport selects on skill rather than size
D. an initial maturity advantage compounds into one no longer about age
E. birth month affects physical development permanently
questions.explanation: Better team, better coaching, and the advantage ceases to be about the months.

questions.passageText:
Until the nineteenth century the finest blue pigment available to European painters was ground from lapis lazuli, mined in what is now Afghanistan and transported across the whole width of the known world. It cost more by weight than gold, and its price shaped painting in ways that are visible on the surviving panels.

Contracts survive that specify the pigment by grade and quantity, sometimes stipulating how many ounces of the best ultramarine were to be used and on which figure. The blue was not a stylistic choice but a purchased commodity, and its concentration on the principal figure records what the patron paid for as much as what the painter intended. Cheaper substitutes existed — azurite, and later smalt — which are physically different, greener and less stable, and which painters used in areas the eye would attend to less.

This has consequences for interpretation. A modern viewer reading a blue robe as a symbolic statement may be reading an economic one, and conservation analysis distinguishing ultramarine from azurite in different parts of a picture recovers information about the commission that no amount of looking supplies.

When synthetic ultramarine was produced in the 1820s at a fraction of the cost, the meaning of the colour changed with its price. What had been a display of expenditure became simply a colour, available to anyone. The pigment on the panel was the same substance; what it communicated was not, which is a reminder that the meaning of a material is partly a fact about its market.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, contracts specifying ultramarine by grade and quantity show that the pigment was
options: A. applied by specialist craftsmen
B. a purchased commodity as much as a stylistic choice
C. unavailable outside Italy
D. reserved for religious subjects by law
E. cheaper than azurite in bulk
questions.explanation: The concentration of the blue on the principal figure records what the patron paid for.

The pigment on the panel was the same substance; what it communicated was not, which is a reminder that the meaning of a material is partly a fact about its market.
